questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: The principal argument for "shifting left" on security is that:
options: Static analysis tools return fewer false positives when run against incomplete code
Remediating a defect becomes exponentially more expensive the later in the SDLC it is discovered
Privacy legislation requires a documented security review before the design phase closes
Defects found after release cluster in third-party components rather than in-house code
questions.explanation: A flaw caught at requirements or design costs a conversation; the same flaw caught after release costs a patch, a re-test, a deployment, possible notification obligations and reputational damage. (C) describes a compliance driver, not the cost argument.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: Which list correctly gives the phases of the Secure SDLC as taught in this course?
options: Requirements → Design → Development → Testing → Deployment → Maintenance
Requirements → Specifications → Design → Development → Testing → Installation → Maintenance
Requirements → Specifications → Design → Development → Integration → Testing & debugging → Installation → Maintenance
Requirements → Threat modelling → Specifications → Design → Development → Integration → Testing & debugging → Installation → Maintenance
questions.explanation: — eight phases — , with findings feeding back to the start. (B) drops Integration; (D) invents a phase — threat modelling happens within Design, it is not a phase of its own.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: Threat modelling is carried out during which SDLC phase?
options: Requirements definition
Design
Determining specifications
Integration
questions.explanation: Design — Threat modelling systematically identifies likely attacks against a proposed architecture, so it must happen while the architecture is still a decision rather than a build. Requirements states that the system must resist attack; Design works out how.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: "Deciding that AES-256 will be used to encrypt medical records at rest" belongs to which phase?
options: Requirements definition
Development
Design
Determining specifications
questions.explanation: Determining specifications — choosing which standard, algorithm or method. Requirements would state "records must be encrypted at rest"; Design decides where in the architecture encryption sits; Development writes the code.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: The distinction between the Design and Development phases is that:
options: Design selects the specific algorithms and standards; Development produces the architecture that uses them
Design produces the architecture and decides which controls will exist; Development implements those controls in code
Design writes and unit-tests the security modules; Development combines them with third-party components
Both phases produce code, and they are distinguished only by whether the code is security-related
questions.explanation: Read the described activity carefully — is it planning/deciding or building? (A) is the specifications/design swap; (C) is the development/integration swap.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: "Closing unused ports and removing default credentials on the production server before go-live" is which phase?
options: Integration
Testing and debugging
Installation
Maintenance
questions.explanation: Installation — This is system hardening at deployment. The same activity performed as ongoing patching after release would be Maintenance — the timing is what decides it.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: Combining a trusted in-house login module with a third-party payment component without creating new weaknesses is the security concern of which phase?
options: Integration
Design
Testing and debugging
Determining specifications
questions.explanation: Integration — Two individually secure components can create a vulnerability at the seam — mismatched trust assumptions, unvalidated data crossing the boundary, or excessive data exposure. Testing would detect such a flaw; Integration is where it is created.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: Which best describes how end users influence secure design?
options: The technical skill, needs and behaviour of the user group determine which controls are usable, and an unusable control is not an effective control
End users determine the cryptographic standards applied to their own data
End users are consulted during Maintenance, once real usage patterns are available
End user influence is limited to reporting defects through the support channel after release
questions.explanation: A control users route around is not a control. Elderly or low-literacy users may need an alternative to biometrics; high-security staff may accept hardware tokens that consumers would abandon. (C) and (D) describe feedback, not influence on design.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: Requiring a complex 16-character password that users then write on a sticky note illustrates:
options: A control that lowers real-world security because it ignores user behaviour
Least privilege applied to credential strength
Defence in depth, where the weakest layer happens to be physical rather than technical
An acceptable trade-off, since the policy still satisfies the confidentiality requirement
questions.explanation: Usability and security are not opposites, but they interact — a policy so demanding that users defeat it has made the system less secure, not more. (C) is a tempting misuse of the term: the sticky note is not a designed layer.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: Which of the following is not one of the five key principles of Security by Design?
options: Threat modelling and risk assessment
Built-in security measures rather than added-on ones
Continuous monitoring and auditing
Remediation of vulnerabilities as they are reported after release
questions.explanation: The five are systematic integration, threat modelling and risk assessment, built-in security measures, continuous monitoring and auditing, and a proactive approach. Reactive remediation is precisely what Security by Design rejects.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: Which triad member is compromised by a successful DDoS attack?
options: Availability
Integrity
Confidentiality
Availability and integrity together, because dropped requests leave transactions half-completed
questions.explanation: Availability — A DoS/DDoS does not read or alter stored data — it prevents authorised users from reaching it. (D) is tempting but describes a consequence of poor transaction design, not the attack's target. Countermeasures: rate limiting, load balancing, CDN filtering, redundant and scalable design.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: A checksum mismatch on a downloaded file indicates a failure of:
options: Confidentiality — the file's contents were exposed in transit
Authentication — the sender's identity cannot be confirmed
Integrity — the file's contents were altered in transit
Non-repudiation — the sender could deny having sent that file
questions.explanation: Integrity — The sender calculates the checksum and sends it with the file; the receiver recalculates and compares. Different values mean the data was altered and the file should be rejected. A checksum says nothing about who sent it — that is (B)'s territory and requires a signature.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: "What can you do once you're logged in?" is the question answered by:
options: Authentication
Authorisation
Accountability
Access control lists
questions.explanation: Authorisation — Authentication asks who are you; accountability asks what did you do. (D) is a trap: an ACL is a mechanism that implements authorisation, not the concept being asked for.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: Which control most directly supports accountability?
options: Role-based access control, which records which role performed each action
Digital signatures, which prove who authored a given document
Multi-factor authentication, which confirms the user is who they claim to be
A comprehensive, tamper-resistant audit log of who did what and when
questions.explanation: Accountability requires a record of access and modification — audit tables, secure logging, SIEM monitoring. (A) controls access rather than recording it; (B) and (C) establish identity, which accountability depends on but is not the same as.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: MFA is described as the single most effective control against broken authentication because:
options: It removes the password from the authentication process entirely
It causes credentials to be stored as salted hashes rather than plaintext
A stolen or guessed password is no longer sufficient on its own to gain access
It forces session tokens to expire after a fixed interval
questions.explanation: MFA combines something you know, have or are, so credential stuffing and brute force fail even when the password is known. (A) describes passwordless authentication, which is a different thing.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: In RBAC, giving an "Editor" the ability to create and edit content but not to delete it is an example of:
options: Authentication, since the role is verified at login
Separation of duties, since editing and deleting are held by different roles
Least privilege implemented through authorisation
Defence in depth, since a second control blocks the deletion
questions.explanation: Least privilege grants the minimum rights needed to do the job. (B) is the strongest trap: separation of duties splits a single sensitive transaction across two people so neither can complete it alone — that is not what is happening here. Access rights must be regularly reviewed as roles change.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: Confidentiality is best achieved through:
options: Encryption at rest and in transit combined with access control
Redundancy and failover, so data survives the loss of a component
Hashing and version control, so any alteration is detectable
Digital signatures, so the origin of the data can be proven
questions.explanation: (C) serves integrity, (B) availability, (D) integrity and non-repudiation. Note that encryption alone is not confidentiality — without access control, anyone with the key can read the data.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: Which pairing is correct?
options: Confidentiality → hashing · Integrity → encryption
Availability → redundancy and failover · Integrity → checksums and version control
Integrity → rate limiting · Availability → load balancing
Confidentiality → checksums · Availability → salting
questions.explanation: Availability = redundancy, failover, backups, scalable design. Integrity = checksums, hashing, version control, secure coding that prevents injection. (A) swaps the two; in (C) only the second half is right — rate limiting serves availability, not integrity.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: Non-repudiation means:
options: The recipient can prove the message was not altered after it was sent
The sender's identity is verified before the message is accepted
The sender cannot later deny having sent or signed the message
The message can be read only by its intended recipient
questions.explanation: Provided by digital signatures — only the holder of the private key could have produced the signature. (A) is integrity, (B) is authentication, (D) is confidentiality. All four are properties a signature scheme touches, which is why this distinction is examined so often.

questions.topic: CIA and AAA
questions.stem: A hospital system must ensure a patient record is accurate and unmodified, is visible only to treating staff, and remains reachable during a power failure. Which triad members are engaged, in that order?
options: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability
Integrity, Availability, Confidentiality
Integrity, Confidentiality, Availability
Availability, Confidentiality, Integrity
questions.explanation: Accurate and unmodified = Integrity; visible only to treating staff = Confidentiality; reachable during a failure = Availability.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: The key difference between encryption and hashing is that:
options: Encryption is reversible with the correct key; hashing is one-way and designed not to be reversed
Encryption is one-way; hashing is reversible with the correct key
Both are reversible, but hashing requires a key pair rather than a single key
Encryption produces a fixed-length output regardless of input; hashing produces variable-length output
questions.explanation: Passwords should be hashed (never decrypted, only compared); data that must be read again must be encrypted. (D) is the reverse of the truth — it is hashing that produces a fixed-length digest.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Salting defeats which specific attack?
options: Precomputed rainbow-table lookups
Brute-force guessing against a single targeted account
Credential stuffing using passwords leaked from another service
Man-in-the-middle interception of the password in transit
questions.explanation: Rainbow tables — A random per-user salt means two users with the same password produce different hashes, so a precomputed table is useless. Salting does not meaningfully slow a brute force against one account (that is what a slow KDF like bcrypt is for), and it does nothing against (C) or (D).

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: AES supports key sizes of:
options: 56, 112 or 168 bits
questions.explanation: 128, 192 or 256 bits — AES is symmetric — one key encrypts and decrypts — and is the standard choice for data at rest. (C) is DES/3DES; (A) is RSA, which is asymmetric.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Which statement about asymmetric encryption is correct?
options: A single shared key both encrypts and decrypts, which is why key distribution is the hard problem
The private key always encrypts and the public key always decrypts, including when confidentiality is the goal
The public key encrypts and the private key decrypts; it is slower than symmetric but solves key distribution
It is faster than symmetric encryption, which is why TLS uses it for the entire session
questions.explanation: (A) describes symmetric encryption. (B) is the sharpest trap: private-key-encrypts is true for digital signatures, but for confidentiality the direction is the other way round — otherwise anyone holding the public key could read the message.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: During the TLS handshake, asymmetric encryption is used to:
options: Verify the server's certificate and agree a shared symmetric session key
Hash the user's password before it is transmitted
Encrypt every packet of the session, since asymmetric encryption is the stronger of the two
Compress the session data before the symmetric cipher is applied
questions.explanation: Browser requests a secure connection → server sends its certificate → browser verifies it against a trusted CA → asymmetric exchange establishes a session key → fast symmetric encryption carries the session.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: A Certificate Authority exists to:
options: Issue and digitally sign certificates so a client can confirm a server is who it claims to be
Generate the symmetric session key used for each TLS connection
Encrypt data at rest on the servers it certifies
Hold an escrow copy of each server's private key for recovery
questions.explanation: Encryption alone stops eavesdropping; the certificate stops impersonation — together they defeat a man-in-the-middle attack. (D) would destroy the entire trust model: the private key never leaves the server.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: In chr((ord(char) - 97 + shift) % 26 + 97), the value 97 is used because:
options: It is the modulus that wraps the shift around the end of the alphabet
It is the ASCII code of uppercase 'A', which the expression normalises the input to
It is the number of printable ASCII characters, keeping the result printable
It is the ASCII code of lowercase 'a', converting the character to a 0-based alphabet index
questions.explanation: ord('a') = 97 and ord('A') = 65. Subtracting 97 gives a 0–25 index, % 26 wraps around the alphabet, then adding 97 back returns to ASCII. (A) confuses 97 with the 26 that is doing the wrapping.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Applying a Caesar cipher with a shift of 3 to "HELLO" produces:
options: "IFMMP"
"KHOOR"
"EBIIL"
"LIPPS"
questions.explanation: "KHOOR" — Each letter shifts forward three positions: H→K, E→H, L→O, L→O, O→R. (A) is a shift of 1, (C) a shift of −3, (D) a shift of 4 — the distractors are all correctly executed cipher operations with the wrong key, so counting carefully is the whole task.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: A digital signature is produced by signing the data with the:
options: Sender's public key
Sender's private key
Recipient's public key
Recipient's private key
questions.explanation: Sender's private key — , and verified by anyone using the sender's public key. This proves authenticity and integrity and provides non-repudiation. Note this is the opposite direction to confidentiality, where you encrypt with the recipient's public key — option (C).

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Encryption at rest and in transit are best described as:
options: At rest is provided by TLS; in transit is provided by AES
At rest protects stored data, typically with symmetric encryption such as AES; in transit protects data crossing a network, typically with TLS
At rest protects data held in memory while the program runs; in transit protects it once written to disk
At rest uses asymmetric encryption because the key can be published; in transit uses symmetric encryption for speed
questions.explanation: A complete answer to "how would you protect this data" covers both — encrypting the database is useless if the login form posts over plain HTTP. (C) inverts the two terms; "at rest" means stored, not resident in RAM.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Fernet in Python's cryptography library provides:
options: Asymmetric key generation for signing and verification
A deliberately slow, salted hash function suitable for storing credentials
Symmetric authenticated encryption — one key both encrypts and decrypts
Parameterised query construction to prevent SQL injection
questions.explanation: It generates a URL-safe base64-encoded 32-byte key and both encrypts and authenticates. (B) describes bcrypt — the trap is that both appear in the same unit; passwords must be hashed, never encrypted.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: An HSM and a KMS both address:
options: Enforcement of password complexity policy across an organisation
Detection of injection payloads in incoming requests
Issuing and distributing TLS certificates to clients
Secure generation, storage and rotation of encryption keys
questions.explanation: An HSM is dedicated tamper-resistant hardware; a KMS (AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS) is a managed cloud service. Both exist because a key hard-coded in source is not a secret. (C) is the role of a Certificate Authority.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Which of the following is not symmetric?
options: Triple DES
AES-256
Fernet
questions.explanation: RSA-2048 — is asymmetric — a public/private key pair. AES, Triple DES and Fernet all use a single shared key for both operations.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: A checksum can detect that a file was altered but cannot:
options: Be generated using a hashing algorithm such as SHA-256
Detect an alteration caused accidentally by transmission error
Be recalculated independently by the receiver
Prove who made the alteration, or prevent it from happening
questions.explanation: A checksum is an integrity detection mechanism only. Attribution requires digital signatures and logging; prevention requires access control. It detects accidental and deliberate alteration equally well, which rules out (B).

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Plaintext is:
options: The output of an encryption algorithm before it is encoded for transmission
Data encrypted with a symmetric rather than an asymmetric key
A fixed-length hash digest of the original data
The readable, unencrypted original data
questions.explanation: Ciphertext is the encrypted form — option (A) describes it. Encryption converts plaintext → ciphertext; decryption reverses it with the key.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: The three purposes of sandboxing are:
options: Validation, sanitisation, error handling
Isolation, containment, eradication
Detection, containment, recovery
Isolation, testing, security
questions.explanation: Isolation (a controlled environment separate from the main system) · testing (safely trial untrusted software) · security (contain malware). (B) and (C) borrow terms from incident response — containment appears in both topics, which is what makes them tempting. Examples: per-tab browser processes, antivirus opening a suspicious file in a VM, app permission prompts, VMs and containers.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: Containerisation (e.g. Docker) is best described as:
options: Encrypting an application's data and configuration at rest
Running an application inside a full guest operating system with its own kernel
Packaging an application with its dependencies so it runs in an isolated, reproducible environment
Restricting what an application may access through the host OS's permission prompts
questions.explanation: It is sandboxing at whole-application level, and it makes environments reproducible between development and production. (B) is a virtual machine — containers share the host kernel, which is the defining difference. (D) is application sandboxing on a phone or desktop.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: The three syllabus principles of Privacy by Design are:
options: Proactive not reactive · embedded into design · respect for user privacy
Privacy as the default setting · end-to-end lifecycle security · visibility and transparency
Collection limitation · purpose limitation · data minimisation
Masking · generalisation · aggregation
questions.explanation: (B) is the sharpest trap — those are genuine Cavoukian principles, just not the three the syllabus names. The full seven add privacy as the default setting, positive-sum, end-to-end lifecycle security, and visibility and transparency. Answer with the three, then add the others as extra depth on a 5+ mark question.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: Replacing an exact age with a range such as "30–35" is which anonymisation technique?
options: Masking
Aggregation
Generalisation
Perturbation
questions.explanation: Generalisation — reducing precision while keeping the record intact. (B) Aggregation would report a single average age for the whole group, losing the individual record entirely; (D) perturbation would add random noise to the true age. The five techniques are masking, pseudonymisation, generalisation, perturbation and aggregation.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: Data minimisation requires that:
options: Personal data is deleted once a fixed retention period expires
Identifying fields are stripped from a dataset before it is analysed
Data is stored in the smallest practical format through compression
Only the data required for the software's stated purpose is collected in the first place
questions.explanation: Data you never collected cannot leak. (A) is storage limitation and (B) is anonymisation — both are real privacy measures, but neither is minimisation, which acts at the point of collection.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: If an organisation wants to use collected data for a purpose other than the one it was collected for, it must first:
options: Obtain the individual's fresh, explicit consent for the new purpose
Update its published privacy policy to list the additional purpose
Encrypt the data so the new use cannot be linked back to individuals
Notify the OAIC of the change of purpose
questions.explanation: Purpose limitation is one of the APPs — use and disclosure is restricted to the purpose for which the data was collected unless fresh consent is obtained. (B) is necessary but not sufficient: silently amending a policy does not create consent.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: How many Australian Privacy Principles are there?
options: 13, under the Privacy Act 1988
8, matching the ASD Essential Eight
7, matching the seven Privacy by Design principles
10, matching the OECD privacy guidelines
questions.explanation: 13 — In outline: open and transparent management, collection for a legitimate purpose, use and disclosure limited to that purpose, rights of access and correction, and reasonable steps to keep data secure.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: Under the NDB scheme, an organisation must notify:
options: The OAIC only, which then decides whether individuals are informed
Affected individuals and the OAIC, for every breach regardless of likely harm
Affected individuals only, unless a government agency is involved
Affected individuals and the OAIC, where the breach is likely to result in serious harm
questions.explanation: The serious harm threshold is the whole point of the distinction — (B) is the most commonly chosen wrong answer. "Notify" is the third step of the four-step breach response: Contain → Assess → Notify → Review.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: PCI-DSS applies to:
options: Any organisation processing the personal data of EU residents
Any system holding health records in NSW
Any system that stores, processes or transmits payment card data
Australian government agencies and their contracted service providers
questions.explanation: (B) is the Health Records and Information Privacy Act 2002 (NSW); (A) is the GDPR. Note PCI-DSS is an industry standard enforced by the card schemes, not legislation.

questions.topic: Sandboxing, privacy and compliance
questions.stem: Which of these is an Australian compliance framework named in the school notes?
options: ASD Essential Eight
SOX
HIPAA
GDPR
questions.explanation: ASD Essential Eight — The Australian instruments in the notes also include the Privacy Act 1988, the NDB scheme, the Health Records and Information Privacy Act 2002 (NSW), Australian Consumer Law, AS/NZS ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002, and the TOLA Act 2018. GDPR appears in the notes but is European. Naming two or three specific instruments beats writing "privacy laws".

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: Business continuity differs from disaster recovery because continuity:
options: Restores systems from backup, while disaster recovery keeps functions running through the event
Keeps critical functions running during and immediately after the disruption, while recovery restores systems afterwards
Is measured by RTO, while disaster recovery is measured by RPO
Applies to data, while disaster recovery applies to infrastructure
questions.explanation: Continuity = automatic failover so customers barely notice. Disaster recovery = rebuilding and restoring from backups after the event. (C) is a plausible-sounding invention — both plans are specified using both RTO and RPO.

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: An organisation states that it can tolerate at most one hour of lost data. This is its:
options: Recovery Time Objective
Recovery Point Objective
Mean Time to Recovery
Maximum Tolerable Downtime
questions.explanation: RPO — the maximum acceptable data loss, which is what sets backup frequency. (A) and (D) are both about time to restore service; (C) is an observed average rather than a target. The tell is "lost data", not "downtime".

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: A failover system:
options: Is a standby that an administrator manually brings online once an outage is confirmed
Copies data to a secondary site at fixed scheduled intervals
Automatically switches to a standby system when the primary fails, minimising downtime
Distributes incoming traffic evenly across all currently available servers
questions.explanation: The word automatically is doing the work — (A) is the same architecture without it, and is not failover. (B) is replication/backup and (D) is load balancing; all three support availability, but only (C) answers the question.

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: The five steps of incident response are:
options: Detect → contain → eradicate → recover → review
Contain → assess → notify → review
Identify → protect → detect → respond → recover
Detect → assess → contain → notify → restore
questions.explanation: (B) is the four-step breach response taught alongside it — note it only has four steps, so the stem itself rules it out. (C) is the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, and (D) is a plausible hybrid of the two real lists.

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: SAST differs from DAST because SAST:
options: Analyses source code, bytecode or binaries without executing the program
Tests a running application from the outside, as an attacker would
Requires a deployed environment and valid test credentials
Is carried out manually by reviewers rather than by automated tooling
questions.explanation: The tell in any question is whether the code is executed. (B) and (C) both describe DAST; (D) describes code review. SAST finds issues early but generates false positives; DAST finds runtime issues but cannot point to the offending line.

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: Bombarding a running application with large volumes of random or malformed input is:
options: Static application security testing
Penetration testing
Fuzzing
Vulnerability assessment
questions.explanation: Fuzzing — a dynamic technique used alongside DAST to trigger crashes that reveal unhandled input paths. (B) is broader and goal-directed; (D) does not execute attacks at all.

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: The difference between a vulnerability assessment and a penetration test is that a vulnerability assessment:
options: Actively exploits weaknesses in order to demonstrate real impact
Examines source code, whereas a penetration test examines the running system
Identifies, quantifies and ranks weaknesses without exploiting them
Is conducted only after a penetration test has established the scope
questions.explanation: Assessment finds and ranks; penetration testing actively exploits. (B) is the SAST/DAST distinction imported into the wrong question — both activities usually target the running system.

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: A stated limitation of code review is that:
options: It detects only syntax errors, not logic errors
It is time-consuming on large codebases and reviewers may still miss subtle issues
It requires the application to be running in a test environment
It can only be carried out by the developer who wrote the code
questions.explanation: Its strengths are human insight, early detection and knowledge sharing. (D) inverts the actual guidance — review should be done by developers other than the author, precisely because the author's assumptions are invisible to them.

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: Which testing strategy could be used earliest in development?
options: Fuzzing
Static application security testing
Dynamic application security testing
Penetration testing
questions.explanation: SAST — it needs only source code, so it can run from the first commits. All three others require something deployed and running, which is the property that orders them in time.

questions.topic: Resilience, recovery and code security strategies
questions.stem: Hardening a system involves:
options: Reducing the attack surface — patching, removing unnecessary services and default accounts, applying least privilege, tightening firewall rules
Encrypting all data at rest and in transit so intercepted data is unreadable
Adding intrusion detection and continuous monitoring to catch attacks in progress
Requiring longer passwords and enforcing periodic rotation
questions.explanation: Every option is a real security measure — only (A) is hardening. The attack surface is the total set of points at which an unauthorised user could try to enter or extract data; hardening shrinks it rather than defending it.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: Validation and sanitisation differ because validation:
options: Encodes input at the moment it is written back into the page
Transforms input into a safe form by stripping or escaping harmful content
Rejects input that does not meet the expected format, type or range
Is performed on the client before submission, whereas sanitisation is performed on the server
questions.explanation: Validation rejects; sanitisation transforms. (A) is output encoding, a third distinct control. (D) is a common invention — both validation and sanitisation must happen server-side.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: Stripping <script> tags from a submitted comment is:
options: Validation
Sanitisation
Output encoding
Whitelisting
questions.explanation: Sanitisation — the input is cleaned and accepted rather than rejected. (C) is the close cousin: output encoding leaves the stored data untouched and renders the tags harmless at display time instead. In a PWA, DOMPurify performs sanitisation before content reaches the DOM.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: The most effective defence against SQL injection is:
options: Escaping single quotes in the input string before the query is assembled
Restricting the application's database account to SELECT-only permissions
Validating the login form's fields in the browser before submission
Using a parameterised query, so user input is bound as data and never parsed as command syntax
questions.explanation: WHERE username = ? with the value bound separately. (A) and (B) are genuine defence-in-depth measures — escaping is fragile and easily bypassed by encoding tricks, and least privilege limits the damage without preventing the injection. (C) is trivially bypassed by sending the request directly.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: The input ' OR '1'='1 in a login field is an attempt at:
options: Cross-site scripting
Path traversal
Command injection
SQL injection
questions.explanation: SQL injection — The leading quote closes the string literal and the appended condition is always true, so the WHERE clause matches every row. (C) would use shell metacharacters such as ; or && rather than SQL syntax.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: Good error handling in a secure application means:
options: Displaying the full stack trace so users can report faults accurately
Showing users a generic message while logging the full detail internally
Catching every exception and continuing silently, so an attacker learns nothing from failures
Returning distinct messages for "no such user" and "wrong password" so users can self-diagnose
questions.explanation: Detailed errors leak schema names, file paths and framework versions — free reconnaissance. (C) sounds security-minded but destroys the audit trail and hides real faults; (D) is user enumeration, which tells an attacker which accounts exist.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: Whitelisting is generally safer than blacklisting because:
options: It is computationally faster than matching against a list of known-bad patterns
It requires less ongoing maintenance as new attack patterns emerge
It permits only explicitly approved input and fails closed, whereas a denylist is always incomplete
It can be applied to file uploads, whereas denylisting cannot
questions.explanation: A newly invented attack string is not yet on any denylist, but it is also not on the allowlist — so it is refused by default. Whitelisting aligns with deny by default and least privilege. (B) is tempting but wrong in both directions: an allowlist needs maintenance too, just not reactive maintenance.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: Which principle should govern what a public API endpoint returns?
options: The full record, so the client retains flexibility over what it displays
Whatever the authenticated user's role permits, with the filtering performed in the client
Only the fields the client actually needs — least privilege applied to data exposure
All non-sensitive fields, with sensitive fields returned in an obfuscated form
questions.explanation: A public product-listing endpoint should never return the supplier's wholesale cost, even though that field sits in the same table. (B) is the classic failure — filtering in the client means the data was still sent; (D) is security by obscurity.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: A JWT is used in API design to:
options: Encrypt the request payload as it travels between client and server
Carry a signed, time-limited proof of identity so credentials need not be resent with every request
Bind a request to the user's origin so forged cross-site requests are rejected
Throttle how many requests a given client may make in a time window
questions.explanation: It supports both authentication (the signature proves who you are) and session management (it expires, forcing re-authentication). Note a standard JWT is signed, not encrypted — its payload is base64, readable by anyone, which rules out (A). (C) describes a CSRF token.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: Relying solely on client-side validation is unsafe because:
options: It cannot check formats such as email addresses or date ranges
An attacker can bypass the browser entirely and send crafted requests straight to the API
It runs before the data is encrypted, exposing the input to interception
JavaScript validation executes more slowly than the equivalent server-side check
questions.explanation: Client-side validation is a usability feature — it gives fast feedback and reduces round trips. Every input must also be validated and sanitised server-side, because the client is under the attacker's control.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: Rate limiting on an API primarily prevents:
options: SQL injection delivered through repeated malformed queries
Brute-force credential attacks and DoS-style overload
Session hijacking, by shortening the window in which a stolen token is valid
Cross-site request forgery originating from an automated third-party site
questions.explanation: It caps the volume of requests, which is exactly what guessing attacks and floods depend on. It is one of the three load-protection measures alongside CAPTCHA and load balancing. (C) is session timeout; a single injected or forged request is unaffected by a rate limit.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: Limiting session data size and lifetime and expiring idle sessions benefits:
options: Security only — the hijacking window narrows, but server load is unchanged
Efficiency only — memory use falls, but the session remains equally exploitable
Neither — session lifetime is a usability setting rather than a technical control
Both security and code efficiency
questions.explanation: Smaller, shorter-lived sessions reduce both the hijacking window and server memory consumption. This dual benefit was directly examined in 2025, and (A) and (B) are each written to look like the "careful" half-answer.

questions.topic: Defensive input handling and safe APIs
questions.stem: Memory management matters for secure, efficient execution because:
options: Garbage collection removes sensitive values from memory as soon as they stop being referenced
Unreleased memory is written to swap, where it can be recovered from disk after shutdown
Faster allocation shortens the window in which an attacker can read data in transit
Memory leaks progressively degrade performance and can eventually crash the system, harming availability
questions.explanation: Buffer overflows — writing past a buffer's bounds — are also a memory-management failure, and a classic vulnerability SAST tools scan for. (A) is the sharpest trap: garbage collection offers no timing guarantee, which is why secrets are explicitly overwritten rather than left for the collector.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: In XSS, the attacker's ultimate target is:
options: The server's database, which the injected script queries directly
The site's DNS records, which the script rewrites
The web server's file system, reached through the script's file access
Other users' browsers, which execute the injected script in the site's context
questions.explanation: The script is stored or reflected by the site and then runs in victims' browsers, stealing cookies or session tokens. The site is the delivery mechanism, not the victim. Countermeasures: sanitisation, output encoding, CSP headers.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: In CSRF, the attacker exploits:
options: The victim's existing authenticated session, causing their browser to send a request they did not intend
A script injected into a trusted page, which then runs with that page's privileges
An unvalidated redirect parameter that sends the victim to an attacker-controlled site
A missing ownership check on a record identifier supplied in the request
questions.explanation: (B) is XSS, (C) is invalid forwarding and redirecting, (D) is IDOR — all four are OWASP-style web vulnerabilities from the same unit. Countermeasures: CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, Origin/Referer verification.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: The clearest way to distinguish XSS from CSRF is:
options: XSS attacks the server's session store; CSRF attacks the rendered page
XSS requires the victim to be authenticated; CSRF works equally well against anonymous visitors
XSS gets the victim's browser to run the attacker's script; CSRF gets it to send a request the victim did not intend
XSS is prevented by CSRF tokens; CSRF is prevented by output encoding
questions.explanation: XSS attacks the page; CSRF abuses the session. Each of (A), (B) and (D) is the correct fact with the two attacks swapped — it is CSRF that requires authentication, and the countermeasures pair the other way round.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: A request parameter directly names a record ID and the server performs no check that the requester owns that record. This is:
options: Broken session management
SQL injection
Insecure Direct Object Reference
Invalid forwarding and redirecting
questions.explanation: IDOR — a form of broken access control, and the core vulnerability in the Optus breach. The fix is an ownership/authorisation check on every request; obscuring or randomising the ID is not a fix.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: Redeeming a one-time discount code many times by firing simultaneous requests exploits:
options: Insecure direct object reference
Broken session management
A race condition
A timing side-channel attack
questions.explanation: Race condition — Every request passes the "unused?" check before any request writes the update. (D) is the closest trap — it also concerns timing, but a side channel leaks information through duration rather than exploiting a check-to-update gap. Countered by record locking, atomic operations and minimising the check-to-update window.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: An application accepts a user-supplied URL in a redirect parameter and sends the browser there. The vulnerability is:
options: Insecure direct object reference
Cross-site request forgery
Path traversal
Invalid forwarding and redirecting
questions.explanation: An attacker crafts a trusted-looking link on the real domain that lands on a phishing site. All four options involve an attacker-controlled parameter, which is what makes them adjacent. Countered by whitelisting permitted destinations and validating targets server-side.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: ../../etc/passwd submitted in a file path field is:
options: Path traversal
Command injection
Invalid forwarding and redirecting
Insecure direct object reference
questions.explanation: Path traversal — manipulating a path to escape the intended directory. (D) is the sharpest near-miss: IDOR also reaches an unauthorised resource, but through a legitimate identifier the server accepts, not by breaking out of a directory. Countered by sanitising file names, storing uploads outside the webroot, and resolving paths against an allowed base.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: Validating an uploaded file by content rather than by extension matters because:
options: Reading the file's magic bytes is faster than parsing and comparing its extension
An executable can simply be renamed .jpg, so the extension proves nothing about the file
The extension is set by the server rather than the client, so it cannot be independently verified
The Australian Privacy Principles require content-level inspection of all uploads
questions.explanation: (C) is inverted — the extension comes from the client, which is exactly why it is untrusted. Also: store uploads outside the webroot, sanitise file names and virus-scan them, because a file the server will execute is a remote code execution risk.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: A login routine that returns "incorrect" the instant it reaches a mismatched character is vulnerable to:
options: A race condition
A brute-force attack
A timing side-channel attack
A rainbow-table attack
questions.explanation: A guess with more correct leading characters takes measurably longer to reject, letting an attacker recover the password one character at a time — reducing the search space from exponential to linear. (A) also involves timing, but concerns concurrent requests rather than measured duration.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: The countermeasure to a timing attack is an isochronous function, which:
options: Introduces a randomised delay before returning its result
Compares the two values faster than a character-by-character loop can
Compares hashes of the two values rather than the values themselves
Takes the same amount of time regardless of the input, so duration carries no information
questions.explanation: Iso-chronous = equal time. (A) is the sharpest trap: randomised delay is a supporting measure that adds noise, but the signal is still there and averages out over enough samples. Other supporting measures: generic error messages, rate limiting, and using established cryptographic libraries rather than hand-rolling comparisons.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: Broken session management is best countered by:
options: Enforcing longer and more complex passwords at registration
Placing the session ID in a URL parameter so that page scripts cannot read it from the cookie store
Regenerating the session ID whenever the user's role changes
Cryptographically random session IDs, short timeouts and invalidation on logout
questions.explanation: (C) is a real control but incomplete — the ID must be regenerated on login as well, or session fixation still works. (B) is backwards: a session ID in a URL is bookmarkable, shareable, logged by proxies and directly editable by the user.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: Phishing is categorised as a user-action vulnerability because:
options: The software contains a coding defect that the phishing message triggers
It is classified by its delivery channel rather than by its underlying technical cause
It requires the attacker to have already compromised the organisation's mail server
The software may be entirely sound; the user is the entry point
questions.explanation: No amount of secure coding prevents a user from typing their password into a convincing replica. Countered by user education, MFA (so a stolen password is insufficient), and email/domain verification — a mix of human and technical controls.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: Which is the #1 item in the OWASP Top 10?
options: Injection
Cryptographic failures
Broken access control
Identification and authentication failures
questions.explanation: Broken access control — users acting outside their intended permissions, e.g. altering a URL to view another account. Cryptographic failures is #2 and injection #3; all four options are genuine Top 10 entries, so the ranking has to be memorised rather than reasoned out.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: SSRF is dangerous partly because:
options: It causes the server to forward the victim's browser to an attacker-controlled site
It executes attacker-supplied script in the browsers of other users of the site
It lets the attacker read files outside the intended directory on the web server
The request originates from inside the trusted network, so it can bypass a firewall, VPN or ACL
questions.explanation: SSRF occurs when an application fetches a remote resource without validating the user-supplied URL, exposing internal services the perimeter was meant to protect. (C) is path traversal and (A) is invalid forwarding — both also involve an attacker-supplied path or URL, which is what makes them tempting.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: "Auto-update functionality that downloads updates without verifying their integrity" is which OWASP category?
options: Software and data integrity failures
Insecure design
Security misconfiguration
Vulnerable and outdated components
questions.explanation: The category also covers relying on plugins or libraries from untrusted sources and insecure content-delivery pipelines — supply-chain risk. (D) is about running a component with a known flaw, not about failing to verify what you install.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: Unchanged default passwords and unnecessary open ports fall under:
options: Insecure design
Security misconfiguration
Identification and authentication failures
Vulnerable and outdated components
questions.explanation: Security misconfiguration — default securities not defined or implemented, including overly informative error messages and misconfigured cloud permissions. (C) is tempting because a default password is involved, but the failure is in the deployment configuration, not in the authentication mechanism itself.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: Insecure design is distinguished from the other OWASP categories because it:
options: Reflects missing security thinking from the outset, and cannot be patched once the system is built
Describes a correct requirement that was implemented incorrectly in code
Describes secure code deployed with unsafe default settings
Describes a sound architecture undermined by an outdated third-party component
questions.explanation: You cannot patch your way out of an architecture that never had a place to put the control. (B) is an implementation defect, (C) is security misconfiguration and (D) is vulnerable and outdated components — three separate categories. This is the direct argument for Security by Design.

questions.topic: User action, file and hardware vulnerabilities
questions.stem: "Logins and failed logins are not recorded, no alerting thresholds exist, and penetration tests trigger no alerts" describes:
options: Security misconfiguration
Security logging and monitoring failures
Insecure design
Broken access control
questions.explanation: (A) is the closest trap, since absent logging is a configuration gap — but OWASP gives monitoring its own category precisely because the consequence is distinct: dwell time. Breaches persist undetected for months because nothing was watching, and there is no forensic record afterwards.

questions.topic: Impact and case study
questions.stem: In the 2022 Optus breach, the underlying technical vulnerability was:
options: A phishing campaign that harvested administrator credentials
An SQL injection flaw in a customer-facing search form
An unauthenticated API endpoint exposing directly referenceable customer identifiers
An unpatched third-party library with a known remote code execution flaw
questions.explanation: An IDOR-style exposure on an endpoint that did not authenticate the requester — approximately 9.8 million records were affected. All four options are causes of real, well-publicised breaches, so the specific case has to be known.

questions.topic: Impact and case study
questions.stem: The most defensible design lesson from the Optus breach is:
options: Replace sequential record identifiers with randomly generated ones so they cannot be enumerated
Authenticate and authorise every endpoint, apply least privilege to the fields returned, and delete data no longer required
Encrypt all customer records at rest, so an exposed endpoint returns unreadable data
Place the API behind a web application firewall configured to block high-volume request patterns
questions.explanation: Each of (A), (C) and (D) is a real control that would have made the attack harder without fixing it. (A) is security by obscurity; (C) fails because the application decrypts data to serve legitimate responses, and the endpoint's responses looked legitimate; (D) treats a design flaw as a traffic problem. Retention was a major aggravating factor — much of the exposed data belonged to former customers.

questions.topic: Impact and case study
questions.stem: A named social/ethical impact of secure software development is digital disruption, meaning:
options: An outage caused by a denial-of-service attack
The loss of service when a deployment fails and must be rolled back
The displacement of workers whose roles are automated by newly deployed software
The way the shift to secure, connected software reshapes industries, business models and communities
questions.explanation: (C) is the trap — that is the employment impact, a sibling consideration rather than a definition of disruption. The full set is digital disruption, employment, privacy, copyright and intellectual property.

questions.topic: Impact and case study
questions.stem: In software engineering, copyright most directly governs:
options: An individual's right to obtain a copy of the data an organisation holds about them
Ownership of a novel algorithm or process, granting exclusive rights for a fixed term
The obligation to hold personal data only for as long as it is needed
Your right to use, modify and redistribute others' code, including open-source licence compliance
questions.explanation: (B) describes patents, not copyright — copyright protects the expression (the code as written), not the underlying idea. Intellectual property is the broader category. You must have the right to use a component before you ship it.

questions.topic: Impact and case study
questions.stem: The strongest argument that secure development benefits an enterprise commercially is:
options: Secure software executes faster, because insecure patterns are usually inefficient ones
It avoids breach costs, regulatory penalties and reputational damage, and builds trust that is very hard to rebuild once lost
It reduces the number of developers required, by eliminating rework
It removes the need for a separate security testing phase later in the SDLC
questions.explanation: Pair it with the shift-left cost argument for a full-mark answer: cheaper to build securely, and vastly cheaper than the alternative outcome. (D) inverts the point — shifting left adds early testing, it does not delete later testing.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: A school portal stores student medical conditions. Which combination best protects it?
options: TLS in transit, RBAC across the whole portal, and daily encrypted backups
AES at rest, TLS in transit, and MFA enforced on all staff accounts
AES at rest, TLS in transit, RBAC restricting medical fields to the nurse and enrolment officer, and audit logging of every access
AES at rest, audit logging, and a web application firewall filtering malicious requests
questions.explanation: All four are credible layered sets — the discriminator is coverage. Only (C) spans confidentiality (encryption plus field-level access control), integrity and accountability (logging who viewed what). (B) authenticates strongly but does not restrict what an authenticated teacher can see; (A) omits encryption at rest and logging; (D) omits transport protection and access control.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: A developer proposes storing passwords with reversible AES encryption "so we can email them to users who forget". The best critique is:
options: Passwords must be hashed and salted, never reversibly encrypted — a recovery flow should reset the password, not reveal it
AES-128 has too short a key for long-term credential storage; AES-256 should be used instead
The passwords should be encrypted with an asymmetric key so only the recovery service can decrypt them
Email is an insecure channel for this, so the password should be sent by SMS instead
questions.explanation: (B), (C) and (D) each "fix" a symptom while leaving the fatal design intact: if the system can read the password, so can anyone who compromises the key. Weak credential recovery is explicitly named under OWASP's identification and authentication failures.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: A team adds MFA but leaves session IDs in the URL. The residual risk is:
options: None — MFA authenticates the user for the whole session
Cross-site request forgery, because a session ID held in a URL cannot carry the SameSite attribute
Credential stuffing, because the URL exposes the username alongside the session ID
Session hijacking, because the identifier is exposed and reusable no matter how strongly the user authenticated
questions.explanation: MFA protects the login; it does nothing once a valid session token leaks into a browser history, a referrer header or a shared link. (B) is a well-constructed distractor — the SameSite claim is technically true but irrelevant, because a URL-borne session ID is not being sent automatically by the browser in the first place.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: Which pair of controls is most appropriate for a public comment field?
options: Rate limiting plus TLS, so the field cannot be flooded and submissions cannot be intercepted
Server-side sanitisation plus output encoding, with a Content Security Policy as defence in depth
Server-side validation rejecting any input containing angle brackets, plus a CSRF token on the form
Hashing each stored comment and verifying the hash before it is displayed
questions.explanation: The threat is stored XSS. Sanitising on input and encoding on output means even a missed payload cannot execute, and CSP limits what could run if both fail. (C) is the near-miss: blocklisting angle brackets is bypassable by encoding, and a CSRF token defends a different attack entirely.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: An organisation runs a penetration test once, passes, and takes no further action for three years. The best criticism is:
options: Penetration tests produce too many false positives to serve as evidence of security
A penetration test is a snapshot in time — new code, new dependencies and new attack techniques all create fresh exposure
A vulnerability assessment should have been run instead, since it ranks findings by severity
Penetration testing must be repeated after every deployment or its results are invalid
questions.explanation: (A) describes SAST, not pen testing — a pen test's findings are demonstrated, so false positives are rare. (D) overstates the point into something no organisation does. Continuous controls — SAST in the pipeline, dependency scanning, monitoring and periodic reassessment — are what maintain security between tests.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: An application shows "Invalid username" and "Invalid password" as separate messages. This is a weakness because:
options: It prevents legitimate users from correcting a mistyped username
It reveals the order in which the application queries its tables
It measurably slows the login response, creating a timing side channel
It confirms to an attacker which usernames exist, halving the work of a credential attack
questions.explanation: Username enumeration. A single generic "Invalid username or password" denies the attacker that information — an application of minimal error messaging. (C) is a related but different failure: the same routine can leak through timing even when the message is generic, which is why isochronous comparison is also needed.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: Which control set best addresses availability for an online exam platform on exam day?
options: Load balancing, autoscaling, rate limiting, a CDN, redundancy and a tested failover, with an RTO agreed in advance
Load balancing, MFA for all candidates, TLS, and hourly encrypted backups
Autoscaling, input validation, RBAC, and a WAF tuned to block automated traffic
Redundant database replicas, checksums on every submitted answer, and full audit logging
questions.explanation: The threat model on exam day is load and outage, not data theft — the controls must match the actual risk. (B) and (C) each contain one availability control padded out with confidentiality measures; (D) is an integrity set wearing an availability disguise.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: A supplier ships a library with a known critical vulnerability. The most appropriate response is:
options: Leave the version in place if the affected function is never called, and document the reasoning
Patch or replace the component promptly, and add dependency scanning to the pipeline so future issues are detected automatically
Add a WAF rule blocking requests matching the published exploit signature
Pin the dependency at its current version, so an unreviewed update cannot introduce further risk
questions.explanation: (A) is a defensible short-term risk acceptance but not a response; (C) mitigates one known payload while the flaw remains; (D) actively makes things worse by guaranteeing the fix is never picked up. "Vulnerable and outdated components" persists because teams do not know what versions they run — an automated inventory and scan is the systemic fix.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: Which statement best demonstrates the evaluate verb applied to a security control?
options: "Against the criteria of breach reduction and usability, MFA is justified — it defeats credential stuffing, the dominant attack on this system — though it adds friction and requires an accessible alternative for users who cannot receive codes; on balance it should be mandatory for staff and optional for customers."
"MFA combines something you know with something you have, so a stolen password alone is insufficient; it is widely deployed and is recommended by the ASD Essential Eight."
"MFA reduces successful account takeovers because an attacker must compromise two independent factors rather than one, which is why credential-stuffing campaigns fail against it."
"MFA and single sign-on both reduce credential risk, but MFA adds an additional factor whereas SSO reduces the number of credentials in circulation."
questions.explanation: Criteria stated, evidence weighed both ways, limitation acknowledged, judgement made. The others are each a different directive verb done well — (B) describes, (C) explains, (D) compares — so length and polish are not the tell.

questions.topic: Application and analysis
questions.stem: Across a single stimulus system, the strongest analytical move is to:
options: Recognise that a real system usually has several distinct vulnerabilities, and match each to a specific countermeasure drawn from the stimulus
Identify the single most serious vulnerability and treat it in depth, since depth earns more than breadth
List every relevant OWASP category with its definition, to demonstrate coverage of the syllabus
Recommend a full redesign under Security by Design, since flaws of this kind are architectural rather than local
questions.explanation: Never assume a stimulus tests only one concept. (B) and (D) are the two most plausible wrong strategies — one under-reads the stimulus, the other escapes into generality. Generic, technically correct answers that ignore the stimulus are the single most-cited marker complaint.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: The cost-of-late-fixes argument supports shifting security left because:
options: A defect caught at design costs a conversation; the same defect after release costs a patch, retest, redeployment and possible notification
Security tools only operate on source code
Developers work faster earlier in a project
Late testing is prohibited under the Privacy Act
questions.explanation: The cost multiplies roughly by an order of magnitude each phase a defect survives — which is the quantified version of the argument markers reward.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: "Identifying that medical data is highly sensitive and must be access-restricted" belongs to which SDLC phase?
options: Determining specifications
Requirements definition
Design
Development
questions.explanation: Requirements asks what data and how sensitive; specifications then selects the encryption standard and authentication method to satisfy it.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: "Selecting role-based access so only the nurse and enrolment officer see medical fields" is:
options: Requirements definition
Maintenance
Integration
Determining specifications
questions.explanation: Specifications chooses the mechanism. Designing where it sits in the architecture is Design; writing the code is Development.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: Checking that a new login module and the existing student database connect without exposing additional fields is:
options: Integration
Development
Testing and debugging
Installation
questions.explanation: Integration — Two individually secure components can create a vulnerability at the seam through mismatched trust assumptions or excessive data exposure.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: Patching the web framework whenever a security update ships is:
options: Installation
Testing and debugging
Integration
Maintenance
questions.explanation: Maintenance — Installation is the one-off hardening at deployment — closing ports, removing default credentials, applying least privilege.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: In the secure SDLC, findings from the final phase:
options: Close the project
Trigger a new specification document only
Are archived without further action
Feed back into requirements definition, making the cycle iterative
questions.explanation: Monitoring and incident findings become next cycle's requirements — the same iterative logic as the project lifecycle.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: An enterprise designs MFA for staff but not for the public-facing student portal used by teenagers. This decision is:
options: Indefensible, since MFA should be universal
A failure of least privilege
Required by the Australian Privacy Principles
A legitimate design response to differing user capability and risk, provided the residual risk is assessed
questions.explanation: End users influence secure design — a control users route around provides no protection. The judgement must still be documented and the residual risk accepted deliberately.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: Which best illustrates end users influencing secure design?
options: Choosing AES-256 over AES-128 for stored records
Enabling TLS on all API traffic
Providing an accessible alternative to biometric login for users who cannot use it
Segmenting the production network from the corporate network
questions.explanation: The other three are technical decisions made without reference to who uses the system.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: Security by Design's proactive approach principle means:
options: Responding rapidly once an incident is detected
Publishing security advisories to users
Anticipating and preventing security events before they occur, rather than remediating afterwards
Purchasing cyber insurance early in the project
questions.explanation: (A) is incident response, which is reactive by definition — the distinction between preventative and remedial is the point.

questions.topic: Benefits, the secure SDLC and end users
questions.stem: Which is not among Security by Design's five principles?
options: Systematic integration
Threat modelling and risk assessment
Continuous monitoring and auditing
Mandatory penetration testing before every release
questions.explanation: The fifth is a proactive approach. Penetration testing is a valuable strategy but is not one of the five named principles.

questions.topic: CIA, AAA and access control
questions.stem: An attacker modifies a stored transaction amount without being detected. The property violated is:
options: Confidentiality
Availability
Integrity
Authentication
questions.explanation: Integrity — Nothing was read by an unauthorised party and the system remained available — the data is simply no longer correct.

questions.topic: CIA, AAA and access control
questions.stem: Which control most directly serves availability?
options: Salting password hashes
Output encoding on user-supplied content
Role-based access control
Redundancy with automatic failover and tested backups
questions.explanation: (A) and (C) serve confidentiality and (B) integrity of the rendered page — the three properties are routinely conflated in answers.

questions.topic: CIA, AAA and access control
questions.stem: "What did you do?" is answered by:
options: Authentication
Accountability
Authorisation
Availability
questions.explanation: Accountability — , implemented through comprehensive logging and an audit trail. Authorisation asks what you can do; accountability records what you did.

questions.topic: CIA, AAA and access control
questions.stem: An audit trail is undermined most seriously by:
options: Storing logs in a separate database
Encrypting logs at rest
Retaining logs for two years
Allowing administrators to edit or delete log entries
questions.explanation: A log the actor can alter is not evidence — which is why append-only or write-once storage and separation of duties matter for accountability.

questions.topic: CIA, AAA and access control
questions.stem: Which is an example of authorisation rather than authentication?
options: Verifying a one-time code from an authenticator app
Confirming a fingerprint matches the enrolled template
Blocking an Editor from deleting a published article
Checking a password against a stored bcrypt hash
questions.explanation: The other three all establish who the user is; only (C) governs what that identity is permitted to do.

questions.topic: CIA, AAA and access control
questions.stem: RBAC is preferred over per-user permissions primarily because it:
options: Requires fewer database tables
Removes the need for authentication
Scales and stays consistent as staff join, change role and leave
Prevents privilege escalation entirely
questions.explanation: Access rights must still be regularly reviewed — RBAC makes the review tractable, it does not make it unnecessary.

questions.topic: CIA, AAA and access control
questions.stem: MFA combines factors from which categories?
options: Something you type, something you click, something you scan
Something you know, somewhere you are, something you own
Something you know, something you have, something you are
Something you remember, something you write, something you say
questions.explanation: Two passwords are not MFA — they are two instances of the same factor, which is the misconception being tested.

questions.topic: CIA, AAA and access control
questions.stem: Non-repudiation is provided specifically by:
options: Hashing the message before transmission
Encrypting the message with the recipient's public key
A digital signature created with the sender's private key
A checksum verified by the receiver
questions.explanation: Only the private key holder could produce the signature. Hashing (A) and checksums (D) give integrity but say nothing about who sent it.

questions.topic: CIA, AAA and access control
questions.stem: In a school portal, requiring the nurse's login and restricting medical fields to that role demonstrates:
options: Authentication and authorisation working together
Authentication only
Accountability and availability
Confidentiality through encryption alone
questions.explanation: Identity establishes who; the role restriction determines what that identity may reach. Encryption would be a third, separate control.

questions.topic: CIA, AAA and access control
questions.stem: The most complete answer to "how would you protect this stored personal data" covers:
options: Encryption at rest only
Hashing the records with a salt
TLS on the login page
Encryption at rest and in transit, access control, logging, backup and a retention limit
questions.explanation: (B) is wrong for data that must be read later — hashing is one-way, so it suits passwords rather than records.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Which statement about salting is correct?
options: The salt must be kept secret in the same way as a key
A unique per-user salt means identical passwords produce different hashes, defeating precomputed tables
Salting makes the hash reversible with the salt
One shared salt for all users is equally effective
questions.explanation: The salt is stored alongside the hash and need not be secret. A single shared salt (D) still allows one rainbow table to be built for that salt.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Passwords should be hashed rather than encrypted because:
options: Hashing is faster than encryption
Encryption cannot be applied to short strings
The system never needs to recover the original — only to compare — so a reversible form is unnecessary risk
Hashing produces a shorter output
questions.explanation: If the system can read the password, so can anyone who compromises the key — which is why "email me my password" is a design smell.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: A digital certificate presented by a server contains:
options: The server's private key
The user's authentication token
The session's symmetric key
The domain name, the public key, an expiry date and the CA's signature
questions.explanation: The private key never leaves the server — including it would defeat the entire scheme, which is what makes (A) the intended trap.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: In the TLS handshake, symmetric encryption takes over after key agreement because:
options: Symmetric encryption is far faster for bulk data
Symmetric encryption is more secure than asymmetric
Asymmetric encryption cannot encrypt large messages at all
The certificate expires after the handshake
questions.explanation: It is a performance decision, not a security ranking — which is why (B) misstates the reason even though the conclusion is right.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: A man-in-the-middle attack is defeated by TLS through two distinct mechanisms:
options: Compression and hashing
Encryption preventing eavesdropping, and certificate verification preventing impersonation
Rate limiting and CAPTCHA
Salting and key rotation
questions.explanation: Encryption alone would still allow an attacker with their own certificate to impersonate the server — both halves are required.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: chr((ord(char) - 65 + shift) % 26 + 65) handles which characters correctly?
options: Lowercase letters only
All printable ASCII
Digits only
Uppercase letters only
questions.explanation: 65 is ord('A'). Lowercase requires 97, and a complete implementation branches on isupper() and islower() and passes other characters through unchanged.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Applying a Caesar shift of 3 to "ZOO" produces:
options: "WLL"
"ARR"
"CRR"
"ZOO"
questions.explanation: "CRR" — Z wraps to C via the modulo — which is exactly what the % 26 exists to handle, and what makes (B) the near-miss.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: ord(char) == 32 tests whether the character is:
options: A digit
A newline
An uppercase letter
A space
questions.explanation: Space — 65 is 'A' and 97 is 'a' — the three ASCII values worth memorising for the Caesar cipher pattern.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: AES is the standard choice for data at rest primarily because it is:
options: Asymmetric, so keys need not be shared
Built into every browser
One-way, so the data cannot be recovered
Symmetric and fast, and the key never needs to cross a network
questions.explanation: Symmetric encryption's key-distribution weakness matters far less when the data never leaves the enterprise's control.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Which is an asymmetric algorithm?
options: AES
DES
RSA
Fernet
questions.explanation: RSA — AES and DES are symmetric block ciphers; Fernet is a symmetric authenticated construction in Python's cryptography library.

questions.topic: Cryptography
questions.stem: Fernet would be an inappropriate choice for:
options: Encrypting a stored configuration file
Protecting a local database of notes
Encrypting a message between two services sharing a key
Storing user passwords
questions.explanation: Passwords must be hashed with an algorithm such as bcrypt, not encrypted — Fernet is reversible by design.
